newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Retrial call after "murdered" men found alive.
newsitem.headline: Retrial call after "murdered" men found alive.

text.p: The lawyer for a Serb soldier jailed after being convicted of killing two Moslem brothers during the Bosnian war said on Thursday he was pressing for a retrial after learning the alleged victims had been found alive.
Sretko Damjanovic was convicted of killing Kasim and Asim Blekic and four other Moslems in a much-publicised war crimes trial in 1993.
The telling evidence against Damjanovic was given by another Serb soldier, Borislav Herak, who was tried with him on genocide charges.
Both Serbs were sentenced to death but the executions were nevr carried out and they are still in prison.
Damjanovic's lawyer said on Thursday he has been pressing for a retrial since December after the discovery that the Blekic brothers were alive and living in Sarajevo.
"The new evidence could clearly lead to my clients' release or conviction for a lesser crime, which is cause for a retrial," lawyer Branko Maric told Reuters.
Herak and Damjanovic were found guilty of genocide and crimes against civilians and prisoners of war while fighting for Serb forces around Sarajevo in 1992.
They were arrested in November 1992 after straying into Bosnian government territory.

Herak confessed to killing Moslem civilians and prisoners of war and to multiple rapes. He testified that Damjanovic killed the Blekic brothers in April 1992 and that his co-defendant had joined him in raping and looting.

"The most powerful evidence against my client was Herak's testimony. So not only does this prove that Damjanovic did not kill the Blekic brothers, it casts doubt on other facts established during the trial," Maric said.
"The only explanation is that my client was beaten into a confession, which he complained about during the trial. Even the court's doctor found scars of physical abuse during the trial."
The Blekic brothers are living along with thousands of Moslem refugees resettled in Sarajevo's bleak northern suburb of Vogosca, which reverted to the Moslem-Croat federation control a year ago.
They fled their frontline family houses in May, 1992, to escape the fighting and lived as refugees in Sarajevo, unaware they had been named as victims of Serb ethnic cleansing.

"The first time I heard I was dead was last summer when Damjanovic's cousin brought a patrol of the (United Nation) international police. I told them that we were the only Blekic family in this region and they took a picture of me," Kasim Blekic said.

Kasim, 43, had known Damjanovic from childhood since both had grown up in the Vogosca area, but he told Reuters he never encountered the man in April or May of 1992 when the murders were supposed to have occurred.
Maric said he had filed a motion in December 1996 for Damjanovic's retrial. The court has not yet replied.
Azra Omeragic, president of the Sarajevo county court, said an evaluation was needed before any decision on a retrial was made. "We have received the motion and we are working on it," she said.
